title: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
summary: Why post-filtered vector search returns too few results, how allow lists, filtered graph walks and planners choose a plan, how match estimates and correlation mislead them, measured on SIFT10K, and multi-tenant layouts.
outcomes: Compute expected survivors and the oversampling needed for k results after post-filtering at selectivity s
Explain how pre-filtering builds an allow list and when a flat scan over the matches is the cheapest exact plan
Explain why filtered HNSW traversal gets stuck or becomes expensive when few vectors match
Describe how Qdrant, Weaviate, Elasticsearch, pgvector and Milvus pick a filtering strategy by selectivity
Estimate match counts under independence and explain how correlated attributes and query correlation mislead planners
Measure recall and cost of filtering plans across selectivities with Faiss and hnswlib, and locate the crossover
Choose a multi-tenant layout (index per tenant, shared filter, per-tenant links, tiered shards) from tenant sizes

lessons.title: Post-filtering: why top-k comes back short

blocks.md:
You finished the HNSW course: a graph search that visits a few hundred vectors instead of millions and returns the approximate top k. Real queries rarely stop there. A shop wants the 10 most similar products **that are in stock and cost under 50**. A RAG app, one that retrieves text chunks and hands them to a language model to answer from, wants the closest chunks **from this tenant's documents**. These conditions on stored attributes are called **metadata filters** (Qdrant calls the stored attributes a *payload*). A filter is also called a **predicate**: a test that is true or false for each vector's metadata.

The examples come from real engines. Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus and Pinecone are vector databases, pgvector is an extension that adds vector indexes to PostgreSQL, and Elasticsearch is a search engine built on Lucene, an open-source search library.

The key number for every filter is its **selectivity** $s$: the fraction of all vectors that pass it. If 10% of products are in NYC, the filter `city = NYC` has $s = 0.1$. Two research papers on filtered vector search come up throughout, Filtered-DiskANN and ACORN; lesson 3 introduces both, and the *Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal* course covers ACORN in depth. The Filtered-DiskANN paper calls the same quantity *specificity* and writes it $|P_f|/|P|$: the number of points that carry filter label f, divided by the number of points in the whole dataset P.

This course says a filter is **restrictive** when $s$ is small (few vectors pass). That matches the ACORN paper and Qdrant's docs, which call a small ratio a *low selectivity*.

Database textbooks sometimes say a filter is *highly selective* when it keeps very few rows, the opposite direction to the ratio. When reading docs, check whether they mean the ratio $s$ or the strictness. Here, small $s$ always means few matches.

The simplest plan is **post-filtering**: run the normal vector search, then drop the hits that fail the filter. Weaviate's docs describe it as a vector search performed first, after which results that do not match are removed. The ANN index never learns about the filter.

The trouble is that the search already truncated its output to a fixed number of candidates before the filter ran. In HNSW that fixed number is the beam width ef from the prerequisite course; pgvector sets it per query with `hnsw.ef_search`, default 40.

blocks.title: pgvector's documented example: 40 candidates, filter city = NYC

scenes.caption: An HNSW scan with pgvector's default `hnsw.ef_search = 40` produces 40 candidates, nearest first. The index has no idea the query also says `WHERE city = 'NYC'`.
The WHERE clause runs afterwards. Here 10% of rows are NYC, and in this draw exactly 4 of the 40 candidates pass, matching the expected 40 x 0.1 = 4.
The query asked for LIMIT 10 and gets 4 rows, even though the table may hold thousands of NYC rows. Nothing failed; the filter simply ran on an already truncated list.

blocks.md:
The pgvector README states this exact case: if a condition matches 10% of rows, with HNSW and the default `hnsw.ef_search` of 40, only 4 rows will match on average.

To reason about it in general, assume each candidate passes the filter independently with probability $s$ (the filter is unrelated to how close a vector is to the query). Then the number of survivors out of $K$ candidates follows a binomial distribution: exactly i survivors has probability K choose i (the ways to pick which i pass), times s to the power i (they pass), times one minus s to the power K minus i (the rest fail).

blocks.tex: \mathbb{E}[\text{survivors}] = K s, \qquad P(\text{zero results}) = (1-s)^{K}, \qquad P(\ge k) = 1 - \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \binom{K}{i} s^{i} (1-s)^{K-i}
blocks.caption: K candidates leave the ANN search, each passes with probability s, the user wants k. Expected survivors: K times s. Zero results: one minus s, to the power K. At least k: one minus the chance of exactly 0, 1, up to k minus 1 survivors. Assumes the filter is independent of distance to the query.

blocks.prompt: A user wants k = 10 NYC results (s = 0.1). You oversample to K = k over s = 100 candidates, so the expected number of survivors is exactly 10. How often does the query actually return all 10?
blocks.reveal: Only about **55%** of the time. The mean of a binomial is its center, so roughly half the draws fall short. To get at least 10 survivors 99% of the time you need **K = 183** candidates, an 18.3x oversample instead of 10x.

blocks.code:
from scipy.stats import binom
k, s = 10, 0.1
print(round(binom.sf(k - 1, 100, s), 3))   # P(at least 10 survive | K = 100)
K = k
while binom.sf(k - 1, K, s) < 0.99:
    K += 1
print(K)                                    # smallest K for 99 percent
blocks.caption: The binomial tail with SciPy: binom.sf(k - 1, K, s) is the probability of at least k survivors out of K candidates. The loop finds the smallest K for 99 percent. Output: 0.549, then 183.

blocks.title: How many of the candidates survive the filter (s = 0.1)

scenes.caption: K = 40 (pgvector default ef_search): the survivors cluster around 4. The chance of reaching the 10 the user wanted is 0.5%.
K = 100, the naive k over s oversample: the mass is centered on 10, so about 45% of queries still come back short.
K = 183: now 99.0% of queries get at least 10 survivors. This is what a 99% guarantee costs when only 1 in 10 vectors matches.
The curve is the oversample that makes the expected survivor count equal k. It grows as 1 over s: halve the selectivity and you must fetch twice as many candidates.
The dots are the K that gives at least 10 survivors with 99% probability, computed from the binomial: 33 at s = 0.5, 183 at s = 0.1, 1874 at s = 0.01. At s = 0.01 that is 187x the k you asked for.

blocks.md: The independence assumption is the optimistic case. If the filter is anti-correlated with the query (the nearest vectors to *winter coats* are rarely in *city = Miami*), the survivors sit even deeper in the ranking. The ACORN paper notes post-filtering's expected cost is about $\log n + k/s$ (k results wanted; $\log n$ is the walk to the query's neighborhood, $k/s$ the candidates read past it) for uniformly spread matches but degrades toward $O(n)$ when matching vectors are far from the query.

Post-filtering leaves the index untouched and is cheap when $s$ is large, but the result count is a random variable. To hold k results you must fetch on the order of $k/s$ candidates, and noticeably more for a high-probability guarantee.

blocks.question: A pgvector query uses HNSW with ef_search = 40, WHERE tenant_id = 7 (0.5% of rows) and LIMIT 10. It usually returns 0 rows. What is the cause?
options: The HNSW graph is corrupted and needs a REINDEX
The filter runs after a 40-candidate scan; with s = 0.005 the expected survivors are 0.2, and P(zero) = 0.995^40 is about 82%
LIMIT 10 is applied before the WHERE clause, so the planner discards matches
HNSW cannot index tables that contain a tenant_id column
blocks.explain: Post-filtering on 40 candidates gives 40 x 0.005 = 0.2 expected matches, and the probability of none is 0.995^40 = 0.82. The index is fine; the filter just sees too few candidates. Iterative scans, a partial index, or a B-tree driven exact scan fix it (lesson 4).

blocks.question: With s = 0.2 and k = 10, roughly how many candidates must leave the ANN search so that at least 10 survive 99% of the time (independent filter)?
options: 50, because k / s = 50
10, because the filter cannot remove the nearest results
About 89
About 500
blocks.explain: k / s = 50 only makes the *mean* equal 10, which gives about 56% success. The binomial calculation gives K = 89 for 99%.

lessons.title: Pre-filtering: allow lists and brute force over the matches

blocks.md:
**Pre-filtering** flips the order: work out which vectors pass the filter *before* any vector search starts. Weaviate's docs define it as determining eligible candidates before the vector search begins, then letting the search consider only candidates on that **allow list**.

Computing the allow list is a classic database problem. An **inverted index** maps each attribute value to the list of object ids that have it (a *posting list*). Weaviate stores these posting lists as Roaring Bitmaps, a compressed bitmap format with fast AND and OR.

blocks.title: Building an allow list from two posting lists

scenes.caption: Twelve objects, ids 0 to 11. The inverted index for `city` gives a bitmap with a 1 for every NYC object: 5 of 12.
The range index for `price` gives a second bitmap: 6 of 12 objects cost under 50.
A bitwise AND yields the allow list: objects 0, 5 and 8 pass both conditions, so s = 3/12 = 0.25. No vector has been touched yet.

blocks.md:
With the allow list in hand there are two ways to use it:

1. **Brute force over the matches**: compute the distance from the query to every allowed vector and keep the k smallest. This is exact (recall 1.0) by construction.
2. **Pass the allow list into the ANN search**, so the graph walk only reports allowed vectors. That is the subject of the next lesson.

The ACORN paper uses option 1 as its pre-filtering baseline and gives its cost as $O(sn + k)$: linear in the number of matching vectors.

Engines choose between the two by the size of the allow list. Lucene makes that choice once per **segment**: it stores an index as several immutable chunks of documents, each with its own HNSW graph.

blocks.title: Pre-filtering pipeline and its two exits

scenes.caption: Step 1: the filter is evaluated against the inverted index, never against vectors. The output is an allow list of roughly s n ids.
Step 2: the engine looks at the size of the allow list. This size is the single number that decides which search is cheaper.

Few matches: compute every distance exactly. Weaviate does this when the allow list is below its flatSearchCutoff (default 40000 objects); Lucene does it per segment when matches are no more than the candidates it examines there.
Many matches: a full scan would cost too much, so the allow list is handed to the HNSW search instead, which only returns ids on the list.

blocks.md: Put numbers on the flat scan. With $n = 1{,}000{,}000$ vectors and $s = 0.001$, the allow list has 1,000 ids and the scan does 1,000 distance computations: cheap and exact. With $s = 0.3$ it does 300,000, which is far more than a typical HNSW query, and it grows linearly with the collection.

blocks.prompt: A Weaviate collection holds 10 million objects with the default flatSearchCutoff of 40000. Query A's filter matches 0.3% of objects, query B's matches 1%. Which one is answered by a flat scan?
blocks.reveal: Query A matches 0.003 x 10,000,000 = **30,000** objects, under the 40,000 cutoff, so Weaviate brute-forces those 30,000 vectors. Query B matches **100,000**, above the cutoff, so it goes through the HNSW index with the allow list. The rule is about the *absolute* count of matches, not the percentage.

blocks.md: A third flavor of pre-filtering builds **one index per filter value**, so a query is routed to an index that only contains matching vectors. The ACORN paper calls this the *oracle partition index*: ideal search quality, but it needs every predicate known in advance. Filtered-DiskANN notes it becomes prohibitively expensive with many labels (the filter values attached to points) or many labels per point. pgvector recommends a cheap version when there are only a few distinct values: a **partial index** such as `CREATE INDEX ... WHERE (category_id = 123)`, which covers only the rows that satisfy its WHERE clause, so every vector in it already passes the filter. For many values it recommends table partitioning, which splits the table into one child table per value, each with its own index.
Pre-filtering with a flat scan is exact and its cost is proportional to the number of matches, $sn$. That makes it the best plan for restrictive filters and the worst plan for broad ones.

blocks.question: Which query is the best fit for pre-filtering followed by a flat scan?
options: 50 million vectors, filter language = en matching 60% of them
2 million vectors, filter user_id = 42 matching 800 vectors
2 million vectors, no filter at all
50 million vectors, filter year > 2000 matching 90% of them
blocks.explain: Brute force costs one distance per matching vector. 800 distances is trivial and exact. The other cases would scan millions of vectors, where a graph search touches only a small fraction.

blocks.question: An engineer says: pre-filtering is always exact, so it is always better than post-filtering. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, exactness always wins
Pre-filtering cannot handle AND conditions
Its flat-scan cost is s n distances, which at broad filters is close to a full scan; post-filtering a graph search is far cheaper when most vectors match
Pre-filtering returns fewer than k results when s is small
blocks.explain: Exactness is not free. At s = 0.6 on 50 million vectors, a flat scan does 30 million distance computations, while post-filtering loses little (60% of candidates survive) at graph-search cost. Pre-filtering never under-fills: it returns k whenever at least k vectors match.

lessons.title: Filtering inside the graph walk, and when the graph falls apart

blocks.md: The middle ground is to filter **during** the graph walk. Elasticsearch documents the `filter` of its kNN search (k nearest neighbors) this way: it is applied during the approximate kNN search to ensure that k matching documents are returned, while filters elsewhere in the query are applied afterwards as post-filters. Weaviate, Qdrant, Lucene and hnswlib all pass an allow list or predicate into the HNSW search.

There are two ways a walk can use the allow list:

- **Strict traversal**: only step onto nodes that pass. The search runs on the *induced subgraph* of matching nodes: the matching nodes plus only the edges that join two of them.
- **Traverse through**: step onto any node to keep navigating, but only allowed nodes may enter the result list. Weaviate's original *sweeping* strategy works like this: a node that fails the filter is skipped and the traversal continues until enough results are found.

A tiny example shows why the difference matters.

blocks.title: A toy graph where the filtered walk gets stuck

scenes.caption: Nine vectors in a proximity graph, entry point E. Colored nodes have city NYC; gray ones are SF. Distances to the query: H 1.26, F 2.53, B 4.47, E 5.4, so the correct filtered top 2 is H then F.
Post-filter with k = 2: the plain search returns I (0.89) and H (1.26). I is in SF and gets dropped, so the user asked for 2 and receives 1.

Strict traversal (only step onto NYC nodes): from E the only NYC neighbor is B, from B only F. F's other neighbors are all SF, so the walk stops and returns F and B. It never reaches H, the true nearest match.

Traverse through: SF nodes may be walked over but never enter the results. Best-first, the walk expands E, C, F, then I, and meets H. The result is H then F, which is correct. Cost: it computed distances to all 9 nodes to return 2.

Make the filter stricter: now only E and H are NYC. Under strict traversal E has no NYC neighbor at all, so the walk returns E alone, the farthest matching vector, while H sits unreachable on the other side.
Traverse through still finds H, but only by walking every SF node. As the matching fraction drops, filtered traversal pays roughly the same k over s price as oversampled post-filtering.

blocks.md:
The strict walk failed because removing the non-matching nodes cut the graph. **Percolation theory**, the study of how a network falls apart as nodes or edges are removed at random, describes when that happens. Qdrant's design article on filterable HNSW cites the classic result for random graphs: there is a critical fraction $p_c = 1/\langle d \rangle$ of nodes, where $\langle d \rangle$ is the average degree (the mean number of edges per node; written d here to keep k for the number of results); keep fewer than that and the network breaks into fragments.

Where 1 over d comes from: keep each node with probability p, then explore outward from a kept node. In this kind of random graph, a node you reach along an edge has about d further neighbors, each kept with probability p, so it leads on to about p times d kept nodes. If p times d is above 1, the exploration keeps branching and one large connected piece spans the graph. Below 1, each round finds fewer new nodes than the last and every piece stays small. The tipping point p times d equals 1 gives $p_c = 1/\langle d \rangle$.

blocks.caption: Simplified: HNSW's bottom layer allows up to 2M neighbors, where M is the per-layer link count from the HNSW course (M = 16 gives 32). With an average degree of 32, the threshold is 1 over 32, about 0.031: a random graph with that degree fragments once fewer than about 3% of nodes remain.

blocks.md: Do not read 3% as a safe threshold. Proximity graphs are not random graphs, matching nodes are often clustered, and being connected is weaker than being *navigable*: greedy search can stall in a matching region long before the subgraph formally splits. Qdrant's docs simply warn that the HNSW graph starts to fall apart when filters are too strict.

Traversing through avoids the disconnection, but look at its cost. If a fraction $s$ of nodes match and they are spread evenly, the walk must visit about $k/s$ nodes to collect k matches: the same $1/s$ scaling as oversampled post-filtering, because it *is* post-filtering done incrementally. Lucene bounds the damage: per segment, if the search visits more nodes than there are matching documents, it stops walking the graph and scores the filtered documents directly.

blocks.prompt: In the toy graph, suppose you ran the strict walk from a second entry point that happens to be H. What would the results be for the first filter (E, B, F, H are NYC)?
blocks.reveal: H's neighbors D, G and I are all SF, so H is isolated in the NYC subgraph. The walk returns H alone: correct first result, missing F. One entry point only ever sees its own fragment. This is why Weaviate's ACORN mode **seeds extra entry points that match the filter** and looks beyond direct neighbors: more ways into each fragment.

blocks.md:
The lasting fixes change how the graph is **built**:

- **Filtered-DiskANN** (Gollapudi et al., WWW 2023) builds a Vamana graph (the graph-building algorithm of DiskANN, Microsoft's index that keeps the graph on SSD for datasets too large for memory) whose edges depend on both geometry and labels, and reports recall close to 100% for filters with specificity as low as $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-6}$.
- **ACORN** (Patel et al., SIGMOD 2024) builds a denser HNSW graph so that the subgraph of nodes passing any predicate stays navigable, then walks only matching nodes. It is *predicate-agnostic*: the filters need not be known at build time. How it is built and searched is the subject of the next course, *Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal*.

- **Qdrant** adds extra HNSW edges for each indexed payload value. Its design article describes the construction: run the same graph-building algorithm inside each category separately, then merge those links into the main graph; the total number of edges grows by no more than 2x, however many categories there are. The docs add that the extra edges only exist if the payload index was created before the graph was built, so indexes should be created before data is loaded.

blocks.title: Qdrant-style extra edges for one payload value

scenes.caption: The toy graph again with the first filter (E, B, F, H are NYC). A strict walk from E goes to B, then F, and stops: H, the nearest match, is never reached.

Build time: run graph construction over the NYC points alone and merge its links. In this toy the NYC-only graph contributes the dashed F to H link. Simplified: real links come from the same neighbor selection as HNSW.
The same strict walk now goes E, B, F, H without stepping on an SF node and returns H then F, the correct filtered top 2.

The limit: links exist per indexed field value, not for every combination of conditions. Under city = NYC AND price < 50, say only E and H pass; F no longer matches, so F to H does not help and E is isolated again.

blocks.md: Qdrant's docs state that limit directly: the extra edges are added for each payload index separately, not for every possible combination of payload indexes. For filters the extra edges do not cover, Qdrant offers an optional ACORN-style search that also looks at neighbors of neighbors when direct neighbors are filtered out, at some cost in speed.

Filtering during traversal is the right default for medium selectivity, but it has two failure modes at low $s$: a strict walk gets cut off (disconnection), and a walk-through degenerates into visiting about $k/s$ nodes. Both point to the same escape hatch: when matches are few, scan them directly.

blocks.question: A strict filtered HNSW walk returns only 3 of the 10 requested results, all far from the query, even though 5,000 vectors match. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The 3 results are the true filtered nearest neighbors
Removing non-matching nodes split the graph, so the walk exhausted the matching fragment around the entry point
The allow list was computed incorrectly by the inverted index
ef is too large
blocks.explain: Five thousand matches exist, so a correct search would return 10. A strict walk can only reach matching nodes connected to its entry through matching nodes. Fixes: traverse through, add filter-aware edges (ACORN, Qdrant), seed matching entry points, or brute-force the matches.

blocks.question: Why does Lucene abandon the graph once it has visited more nodes than there are matching documents?
options: A flat scan costs one distance per match, a bound the walk has already exceeded, and it is exact
Lucene graphs cannot hold more nodes than the filter matches
Visiting too many nodes corrupts the HNSW index
The kNN filter is converted into a post_filter
blocks.explain: Brute force costs one distance per matching document. Once the walk has spent more distance computations than that, the graph is doing worse than a scan would, so Lucene switches to a plan with a known, bounded cost that is also exact.

lessons.title: Query planners: choosing a strategy by selectivity

blocks.md:
Each strategy wins in a different range of $s$. A **query planner** estimates how many vectors match, then picks. A simple cost model makes the tradeoff visible: count distance computations.

- Brute force over the matches costs $sn$.
- A graph search that must surface k matches (post-filter or traverse-through) costs about $c \cdot k/s$, where $c$ is how many distance computations the graph spends per candidate it produces. The $k/s$ shape follows the ACORN paper's analysis; $c$ is an assumed constant you can vary.

blocks.title: Cost model: brute force vs graph search by selectivity

curves.label: graph filling ef: c ef / s

scenes.caption: Simplified model, n = 1,000,000, k = 10, c = 10. Brute force rises linearly with s; the graph cost falls as 1 over s. They cross where s n = c k / s.

Multiply both sides by s, divide by n: s squared equals c k over n, so the crossover is s = the square root of 100 over 1,000,000 = 0.01, where both cost 10,000. At s = 0.001 brute force costs 1,000 vs 100,000; at s = 0.1 the graph costs 1,000 vs 100,000.
A planner takes the lower curve. Grow n to 10 million and the crossover moves left to about 0.003: a bigger collection makes brute force expensive sooner, so the switch happens at a smaller fraction.

Refinement: a walk that fills its whole beam of ef = 40 with matches before stopping pays c x 40 / s. That curve is 4x higher, and the crossover moves right by the square root of 4: s = 0.02, at 20,000 distance computations.
show: graph filling ef: c ef / s

blocks.prompt: In the model, what happens to the crossover selectivity if you ask for k = 100 instead of k = 10 (n = 1,000,000, c = 10)?
blocks.reveal: It moves to the square root of 10 x 100 over 1,000,000 = **0.032**. Asking for more results makes the graph path pay for more candidates, so brute force stays the better choice up to a broader filter.

blocks.md: Two refinements that the simple model hides. First, the beam: an HNSW search keeps ef candidates (the prerequisite's beam width), so even an unfiltered query at $s = 1$ does on the order of $c \cdot ef$ distance computations, never fewer. Second, the stopping rule: hnswlib's filtered search only stops once its result list holds ef allowed nodes (or it runs out of nodes), so it pays about $c \cdot ef / s$ rather than $c \cdot k / s$. With ef = 40 and k = 10 that is 4 times the cost, and since the crossover is $\sqrt{c \cdot ef / n}$ it moves right by a factor of 2. Lesson 6 measures $c$ and the crossover on real data.

Real engines encode the same idea with concrete thresholds:

- **Qdrant** plans per segment, since it too stores a collection as several segments, each with its own indexes. It estimates the filter's cardinality, the number of points that match, from payload indexes (indexes on payload fields); if it is below `full_scan_threshold` (default 10000, measured in KB, where the docs equate one kilobyte with one 256-dim vector, because 256 float32 values at 4 bytes each are 1,024 bytes) it retrieves matching points through the payload index and scores them all. Otherwise it uses the filterable HNSW. Optional ACORN search (off by default) applies when selectivity is below `max_selectivity` (default 0.4); the docs say it is typically 2 to 10x slower but improves recall.
- **Weaviate** pre-filters with an allow list, switches to a flat scan below `flatSearchCutoff` (default 40000), and uses the ACORN filter strategy by default in current versions. A newer `pathseer` strategy walks like sweeping but, while results fill, checks the filter on neighbors of neighbors and scores only matches.

blocks.title: A simplified Qdrant-style planner

scenes.caption: 1,000,000 vectors of 768 float32 dims (3 KB each). Filter estimate: 2,000 matches. 2,000 x 3 = 6,000 KB is under 10,000 KB, so the planner scans those 2,000 exactly.
Estimate 50,000 matches: 150,000 KB, too much to scan. Selectivity 0.05 is below 0.4, and ACORN is enabled, so the planner chooses ACORN to avoid a broken subgraph.
Estimate 600,000 matches (s = 0.6): plain filtered HNSW handles a broad filter well. Simplified: real Qdrant also weighs index availability and condition complexity, and its heuristics may change.

blocks.md: - **Elasticsearch** applies the kNN `filter` during the HNSW search. Elasticsearch splits an index into **shards**, independent pieces that can sit on different machines, and each shard is a Lucene index made of segments. `num_candidates` (per shard, default 1.5 x k, at most 10,000) sets how many candidates are considered. Lucene falls back to brute force per segment when the matching documents are no more than the candidates it would examine in that segment (num_candidates with one segment, else a pro-rata share), or when the walk visits more nodes than there are matches. For indices created in 9.1 or later, Elasticsearch also applies an ACORN-style filter heuristic by default that scores only vectors passing the filter; the *Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal* course covers it.

- **pgvector** post-filters: approximate index scans apply WHERE after the scan. Since 0.8.0, `hnsw.iterative_scan` (`strict_order` or `relaxed_order`) keeps scanning more of the index until enough rows pass, bounded by `hnsw.max_scan_tuples` (default 20,000). For restrictive filters the README suggests a B-tree index on the filter column so Postgres can run an exact scan.
- **Milvus** by default filters entities (its name for rows) first and runs the ANN search within them; an `iterative_filter` hint instead searches in rounds and filters until topK is reached.
- **Pinecone** takes the metadata filter inside the query and returns the top_k most similar records that match it.

IVF indexes (Faiss IVF, Milvus IVF indexes, pgvector's `ivfflat`) filter differently. Recall from the prerequisite that IVF assigns each vector to one of nlist lists and a query scans every vector in its nprobe nearest lists. Faiss's wiki says ids are not pre-filtered but checked as the IVF scanner walks the codes, so only matches inside the probed lists can be returned. If matches are spread evenly, the probed lists hold about

blocks.caption: s n vectors match in total; each list holds about a 1 over nlist share of them, and the query reads nprobe lists. If this is below k, the query comes back short, just like post-filtering.

blocks.title: IVF with a filter: 12 lists, 3 probed, s = 0.02

scenes.caption: 1,200 vectors in 12 lists of 100. A filter with s = 0.02 matches 25 of them; each cell counts the matches in one list (drawn at random by script).
nprobe = 3: the query scans lists 4, 9 and 1, its nearest centroids: 300 vectors, 7 matches. The formula expected 0.02 x 1,200 x 3/12 = 6. The user asked for 10 and gets 7.
An iterative scan probes the next nearest list, 7, and reaches 10 matches. pgvector does this with `ivfflat.iterative_scan`, bounded by `ivfflat.max_probes`; its default `ivfflat.probes` is 1.

blocks.md: When results are short in production, check three things in order: is the engine post-filtering (pgvector without iterative scans, Elasticsearch filters placed outside the `knn` clause)? Is the filter field indexed so the planner can estimate cardinality (Qdrant payload index, Weaviate filterable index)? Is the filter anti-correlated with typical queries? The fix differs for each.

No single plan wins everywhere. Broad filters favor graph search with the filter applied during or after it; restrictive filters favor brute force over an allow list; the middle is where graphs fragment and filter-aware indexes like ACORN and Filtered-DiskANN earn their keep. The deciding input is the estimated number of matches.

blocks.question: An Elasticsearch shard holds a single segment, k = 10 and default num_candidates. The kNN filter matches 12 documents in that segment. What does Lucene do?
options: Walks the HNSW graph and returns at most 10 of the 12
Skips the graph and scores the 12 matching documents directly
Runs the unfiltered search, then applies the filter as a post-filter
Raises an error because matches are fewer than num_candidates
blocks.explain: Default num_candidates is 1.5 x 10 = 15. Since 12 matches is no more than 15, Lucene's documented rule skips the graph and brute-forces the 12 filtered documents for that segment.

blocks.question: Your pgvector query with WHERE category_id = 123 (one of 5 categories, about 20% of rows) returns too few rows. Which fix targets the root cause most directly?
options: Lower hnsw.ef_search to 10
Drop the HNSW index
Increase LIMIT
Enable hnsw.iterative_scan or build a partial HNSW index WHERE category_id = 123
blocks.explain: The shortfall comes from post-filtering a fixed candidate list. Iterative scans keep fetching until enough rows pass; with only a few distinct values, a partial index per value makes every candidate a match. Lowering ef_search makes it worse, and LIMIT does not change how many candidates are scanned.

blocks.md:
Lesson 4 ended on one input: the number of vectors that match. Take a catalog of 10 million products and the filter `city = Miami AND category = swimwear`. If 10% of products are in Miami and 1% are swimwear, how many match both? Multiplying gives 0.1 x 0.01 = 0.001, so 10,000. But Miami sells far more swimwear than the average city: if 5% of Miami products are swimwear, the true count is 50,000, five times the guess.

This lesson is about where match counts come from, when they are exact, how they go wrong, and a second property of a filter that the count misses entirely.

Some engines never estimate. Weaviate builds the allow list from Roaring Bitmaps before searching, so the size it compares with `flatSearchCutoff` is the exact count. Lucene likewise knows how many documents match in each segment before choosing between the graph and a scan.

Others must decide from statistics. PostgreSQL, which runs pgvector, plans before executing, using per-column statistics: most common values with their frequencies for equality, and equal-frequency histograms for ranges: with 10 buckets each holding 10% of rows, `price < 50` where 50 sits halfway through the third bucket is estimated at 2.5 buckets, 25%, by linear interpolation inside that bucket. Qdrant's docs say its payload indexes are also used to estimate filter cardinality accurately, which is why filtering on unindexed fields hurts planning.

The hard case is a combination of conditions. With only per-field counts, an estimator has to assume how the fields relate, and the usual assumption is **independence**: knowing a product is in Miami tells you nothing about its category. PostgreSQL's docs state it plainly: the planner assumes the two conditions are independent, so their selectivities are multiplied. Qdrant's source code does the same for `must` (AND) conditions and uses the complement rule for `should` (OR).

blocks.caption: Under independence, the chance of passing both is the product. For OR, a vector fails only if it fails both, with probability (1 - s1)(1 - s2); one minus that gives the OR rule.

blocks.title: Miami AND category: estimate vs true count (10M products)

scenes.caption: Positively correlated attributes: Miami (10%) and swimwear (1%). Independence predicts 10,000; the true count is 50,000 because 5% of Miami products are swimwear. The estimate is 5x too low.
Negatively correlated attributes: winter coats are 5% of the catalog but only 0.08% of Miami products. Independence predicts 0.1 x 0.05 x 10 million = 50,000; the truth is 800, 62x too high.

blocks.title: Lesson 4's cost model at the estimated and true selectivity

scenes.caption: n = 10 million, k = 10, c = 10: the curves cross at s = 0.0032 (31,623 matches). Swimwear's estimate, s = 0.001, sits left of it: the planner picks brute force, expecting 10,000 distances.
Swimwear's true s is 0.005: brute force costs 50,000 where the graph would cost 20,000. Underestimating cost 2.5x, but the scan is still exact and linear in the true count.
Coats: the estimate s = 0.005 says graph (20,000 vs 50,000). At the true s = 0.00008 the graph walk costs 10 x 10 / 0.00008 = 1,250,000, against 800 for brute force: 1,562x worse.

blocks.md: The two errors are not symmetric. An **underestimate** sends a broad filter to brute force, which costs one distance per true match: more than planned, but bounded and exact. An **overestimate** sends a restrictive filter to the graph, where cost grows as 1 over the *true* s and a strict walk may also fragment (lesson 3). Weaviate's exact allow-list count avoids both, at the price of building the allow list first.

blocks.prompt: A Qdrant segment holds 1,000,000 points of 768-d float32 (3 KB each), so the default 10,000 KB threshold is 3,333 points. A filter truly matches 800. Neither bound decides, so Qdrant samples up to 1,000 points. How often does it end up choosing the graph?
blocks.reveal: Expected hits in 1,000 samples are 0.8, and the interval cannot separate 800 from 3,333 that fast. After the last sample it compares its point estimate, (hits + 2) / 1,004 x 1,000,000, with the threshold: zero hits gives 1,992 and one hit 2,988 (scan), two or more give 3,984 or more (graph). A lucky early pair of hits can also end sampling early in favor of the graph. Rerunning the source's logic 5,000 times in a script, about **20%** of runs chose the graph for this 800-match filter. On the 10-million-point segment from the text it is worse: zero hits already estimate 19,920, so sampling always picks the graph.

blocks.md:
Everything so far counts matches. A second property is **where** they are. The ACORN paper defines *query correlation*: compare how far the query is from its nearest matching vector with how far it would be from the nearest member of a random set of the same size. Matches closer than random is **positive** correlation; farther is **negative**.

Weaviate's blog gives the intuition with a ring shop: search *diamond rings* with a high price filter and most nearby results pass; with a very low price filter, almost none of the nearest neighbors pass, though the filter's selectivity may be the same.

blocks.title: Candidates a perfect post-filter reads for 10 matches (SIFT10K)

scenes.caption: s = 0.1, median over 100 queries of the exact rank of the 10th matching vector. Uncorrelated (random 10%): 101.5, close to k / s = 100. Positive (the clusters nearest the query): 10. Negative (the farthest clusters): 5,710.5.
s = 0.01: positive 27.5, uncorrelated 985, negative 8,482 of the 10,000 vectors. Same selectivity, a 300x spread. Built by our script: 100 k-means clusters, filters made of whole clusters.

blocks.md: Every rule in lesson 1, $K \approx k/s$, assumed the uncorrelated middle bar. The ACORN paper's analysis says the same: post-filtering costs about $\log n + k/s$ when matches are spread uniformly, near $\log n + k$ when they sit next to the query, and up to $O(n)$ when they are far. In its experiments with three LAION workloads, the gap between post-filtering and ACORN was largest under negative correlation, since post-filtering cannot route toward passing nodes. Weaviate's tests found its sweeping strategy still faster than ACORN for highly correlated filters, and ACORN an order of magnitude faster for very low correlation.

A planner's match count says nothing about correlation. Two filters with the same s can need about 30 candidates or 8,500. If a filter's meaning is tied to the embedding (a topic, a language, a source), expect it to be correlated with queries, positively for some and negatively for others.

Exact counts come from a materialized allow list or a single posting list; combined conditions are estimated under independence, which fails on correlated attributes. Overestimates are the dangerous error. Separately, query correlation moves the true post-filter cost far from k / s in either direction.

blocks.question: A planner using lesson 4's cost model (n = 10 million, k = 10, c = 10) estimates 50,000 matches, but only 800 vectors truly match. Which plan runs, and what does it cost?
options: Brute force, 800 distances, since the plan is always fixed after execution starts
Brute force, 50,000 distances, because the planner trusts the estimate
The graph walk, about 20,000 distances, exactly as estimated
The graph walk: chosen because 20,000 beats 50,000 at the estimated s, but at the true s = 0.00008 it costs about 1,250,000 instead of the 800 brute force needs
blocks.explain: At the estimate s = 0.005 the model gives brute force 50,000 and graph 10 x 10 / 0.005 = 20,000, so it picks the graph. The walk's real cost follows the true s: 100 / 0.00008 = 1,250,000. Brute force on the true count would have cost 800.

blocks.question: Two filters each match 1% of a collection. For filter A, the 10th matching vector by exact distance is typically rank 30; for B, rank 8,000. What explains the difference?
options: Query correlation: A's matches cluster near typical queries, B's sit far from them
B has a higher selectivity than A
A's posting list is compressed with Roaring Bitmaps and B's is not
The HNSW graph is disconnected for A but not for B
blocks.explain: Both have s = 0.01, so the uncorrelated expectation is about k / s = 1,000. A is positively correlated with queries and B negatively. Rank by exact distance is a property of the data, not of any index or bitmap.

lessons.title: Measure it: recall and cost versus selectivity

blocks.md:
Time to check the theory on real vectors. The prerequisite measured filters on a hand-built graph; here the same data runs through two libraries. The dataset is **SIFT10K**: 10,000 base vectors and 100 queries of 128-d image descriptors. Each query gets a filter at s from 0.5 down to 0.005 (matching rows chosen at random), and four plans answer it with k = 10. Recall@10 is measured against the exact answer, the 10 nearest *matching* vectors. Every number below comes from one run of these scripts on one machine (random filters from a fixed seed); a rerun with other filters moves them a little.

- **Pre-filter**: brute force over the matches (also the ground truth).
- **Post-filter, over-fetch**: an unfiltered Faiss HNSW search for $K = \lceil k/s \rceil$ candidates, as the ACORN paper's baseline does, then the filter.
- **Faiss selector**: Faiss HNSW given an `IDSelectorBitmap`.
- **hnswlib filter**: hnswlib's `knn_query` with a filter function.

blocks.code:
import math, numpy as np, faiss, hnswlib
def fvecs(p):
    a = np.fromfile(p, dtype="int32")
    return a.reshape(-1, a[0] + 1)[:, 1:].copy().view("float32")
xb = fvecs("siftsmall/siftsmall_base.fvecs")
xq = fvecs("siftsmall/siftsmall_query.fvecs")
(n, d), k = xb.shape, 10
fx = faiss.IndexHNSWFlat(d, 16); fx.hnsw.efConstruction = 40; fx.add(xb)
hl = hnswlib.Index(space="l2", dim=d)
hl.init_index(max_elements=n, M=16, ef_construction=100, random_seed=1)
hl.add_items(xb, np.arange(n), num_threads=1); hl.set_ef(40)
blocks.caption: Setup: load SIFT10K (fvecs format: each row is its dimension, then the floats), build a Faiss HNSW (M = 16, efConstruction = 40) and an hnswlib HNSW (M = 16, ef_construction = 100), search beam 40 in both.

blocks.code:
HP = faiss.SearchParametersHNSW
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for s in [0.5, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02, 0.01, 0.005]:
    tot = np.zeros((4, 3))
    for q in xq[:, None]:
        m = np.zeros(n, bool)
        m[rng.choice(n, round(s * n), replace=False)] = True
        ids = np.where(m)[0]  # pre-filter: exact
        truth = set(ids[np.argsort(((xb[ids] - q) ** 2).sum(1))[:k]])
        K = math.ceil(k / s)  # post-filter, over-fetch
        I = fx.search(q, K, params=HP(efSearch=max(K, 40)))[1][0]
        post = [i for i in I if m[i]][:k]
        b = np.packbits(m, bitorder="little")  # Faiss selector
        sel = faiss.IDSelectorBitmap(n, faiss.swig_ptr(b))
        I = fx.search(q, k, params=HP(sel=sel, efSearch=40))[1][0]
        fs = [i for i in I if i >= 0]
        calls = [0]
        def allow(i):  # hnswlib filter
            calls[0] += 1
            return bool(m[i])
        hs = hl.knn_query(q, k=k, num_threads=1, filter=allow)[0][0]
        for j, (r, c) in enumerate([(truth, len(ids)), (post, K),
                                    (fs, 0), (hs, calls[0])]):
            tot[j] += [len(truth & set(r)) / k, len(r), c]
    print(s, (tot / len(xq)).round(2).tolist())
blocks.caption: The loop. Each row printed is [recall, results returned, cost] for pre-filter, over-fetch, Faiss selector and hnswlib. Cost is matches scanned, candidates fetched, 0 for the Faiss selector (its distances were counted in a separate run), or hnswlib filter calls. Ran in a venv with OMP_NUM_THREADS=2.

blocks.md: The two libraries implement *filter in the graph* differently, and the source code shows how. Faiss's HNSW search pushes every neighbor onto its candidate queue whether or not it passes; the selector is only checked when adding to the results. So the walk is identical to an unfiltered one: in a separate run with Faiss's counters it computed 390.5 distances per query at every selectivity (about 345 on the bottom layer, the rest in the greedy descent through the upper layers). hnswlib only stops once its result list holds ef *allowed* nodes, so it keeps walking as s falls. That is the *walk all nodes, keep matching* strategy from the prerequisite.

scenes.caption: s = 0.1: over-fetching 100 candidates returns 8.73 rows on average (recall 86.2%); the Faiss selector finds 10 matches among the roughly 345 nodes it scores on the bottom layer, but only 86.4% of the right ones; hnswlib gets 100%.
s = 0.01 (100 matches): over-fetch still averages 9.01 rows, recall 90.1%. The Faiss selector's fixed walk now holds 3.84 matches on average: recall 33.8%. hnswlib keeps 99.9% by walking further.
s = 0.005 (50 matches): Faiss selector returns 1.56 rows, recall 15.1%. Over-fetch holds 89.2% by reading 2,000 candidates; hnswlib holds 100%. Recall is only half the story.

blocks.md: Over-fetching to $K = k/s$ returns about 9 rows, not 10: lesson 1's binomial says the mean-only oversample falls short about half the time, and the candidates themselves are approximate. Now the cost side. hnswlib's filter calls were 645 at s = 0.1, 4,386 at s = 0.01 and 8,494 at s = 0.005, out of 10,000 vectors. They undercount the work: hnswlib calls the filter only for a scored node that could enter its result list. Replaying its search loop on the same graph (the replay reproduces those filter counts exactly) gives 1,927, 5,177 and 9,746 distance computations. Pre-filtering costs exactly $sn$: 1,000, 100 and 50.

blocks.title: Measured cost: hnswlib filter calls vs pre-filter (SIFT10K)

y.label: filter calls or distances per query

scenes.caption: Dots: measured hnswlib filter calls. Line a: pre-filter's s n. The lines cross between s = 0.1 (645 vs 1,000) and s = 0.05 (1,153 vs 500); interpolating gives about 0.08. Counting distances instead, hnswlib crosses near 0.15.

Fit lesson 4's model, ef in the numerator, to the filter calls: at s = 0.005 to 0.02, c = 1.13 matches, so c ef = 45. Predicted crossover: the square root of 45 / 10,000 = 0.067, close to the 0.08 where the filter calls cross.

At high s the dots sit above the c = 1.13 line; matching the s = 0.5 dot takes c = 2.1, shown here. The walk's fixed cost of reaching the query's neighborhood dominates there: the floor lesson 4 described.

blocks.md:
Lesson 4's constants, $c = 10$ and $k = 10$, put the crossover at $\sqrt{100/10{,}000} = 0.1$ for this n; the product fitted to hnswlib's filter calls, $c \cdot ef = 45$, gives 0.067, but the distances hnswlib actually computes cross pre-filtering at about 0.15. Extrapolating the fit to a million vectors gives about 0.0067; treat that as a guess and a lower bound: it leaves out the walk's fixed cost, and the number of hops grows with n, so c does too. Measure on your own data.

The full script also builds filters correlated with the query, as in lesson 5, and an IVF index (nlist = 100, nprobe = 10, about 1,086 vectors scanned per query).

blocks.title: Recall@10 at s = 0.01 by query correlation (SIFT10K)

scenes.caption: Positive: matches are the clusters nearest each query. Even a plain 40-candidate post-filter keeps 87.5%; every plan works.

Uncorrelated: the 40-candidate post-filter returned 0.65 rows in this run (0.4 expected; recall 6.5%), IVF returns 8.82 rows (recall 64.4%) from about 11 matches in its 1,086 scanned vectors, and hnswlib stays at 100%.

Negative: matches are the farthest clusters. Every plan that reads a fixed neighborhood returns nothing. hnswlib still reaches 100%, but only after 9,687 filter calls, nearly the whole collection; pre-filter needed 100.

blocks.md:
IVF matched lesson 4's formula: with random filters, the probed lists held on average 5.4 matches at s = 0.005, against $0.005 \times 10{,}000 \times 10/100 = 5$ predicted, and the search returned 5.37 rows.

Timings on this machine (Apple Silicon, two threads), per query at s = 0.01 (two runs): the NumPy pre-filter scan took about 0.03 ms, the Faiss selector search about 0.03 ms, and over-fetching 1,000 candidates about 1.5 ms. The hnswlib times are not comparable, because its filter here is a Python function called once per node.

Report three numbers per plan and selectivity: recall against brute force over the matches, the average count returned (a short result is a silent recall loss), and the work done. Run correlated and uncorrelated filters separately; an average over both hides the failure.

Measured on SIFT10K in this run, the cost model's shape held: hnswlib's filter calls grow as ef / s at low s, brute force as s n, and the crossover sat near where the fitted constant predicts. Counting every distance moves it to about 0.15, because the walk has a fixed cost. Libraries that call themselves filtered search differ: Faiss's selector keeps a fixed walk and loses results; hnswlib keeps recall and pays in nodes visited.

blocks.question: Your measured crossover between brute force and a filtered graph walk is s = 0.05, but lesson 4's model with c = 10, k = 10 predicted 0.01 for your n. What most likely went wrong in the model?
options: n was counted in bytes instead of vectors
Brute force is not linear in s n
The crossover cannot be measured, only modeled
The graph term's numerator: the walk fills ef slots and spends more per candidate than assumed, so c times k should be about 25x larger
blocks.explain: The crossover is the square root of (c times numerator) over n, so a 5x higher crossover means the product is 25x larger. A walk that fills ef = 40 slots instead of k = 10 accounts for 4x, and the rest comes from the per-candidate constant c. Brute force really is linear.

blocks.question: Faiss HNSW with an IDSelector returns 1.56 of 10 results at s = 0.005, while the same graph with no filter returns 10. Why?
options: The selector is checked only when adding results; the walk is the unfiltered one, so only matches among the roughly 345 nodes it scores on the bottom layer can be returned
IDSelectorBitmap only works with IVF indexes
The selector makes Faiss skip non-matching nodes, which disconnects the graph
Faiss caps filtered results at k times s
blocks.explain: In Faiss's HNSW.cpp every neighbor is pushed onto the candidate queue regardless of the selector; the selector gates only the result heap. The walk is the same as unfiltered: 390.5 distances, about 345 of them on the bottom layer where results are collected, so at s = 0.005 about 1.7 of those nodes match. Raising efSearch widens the walk.

blocks.md:
A support-chat company runs one RAG app for 10,000 customer companies. Every query carries `tenant_id = X`, and a result from another tenant is a data leak, not a recall loss. The **tenant** filter is the most common metadata filter in practice, and it has two features ordinary filters lack: it is on every query, and its selectivities are wildly uneven, because a few customers are huge and most are tiny.

That is why engines ship dedicated features for it. This lesson compares the layouts they offer and runs the numbers on a skewed tenant population.

Four layouts:

1. **One index per tenant** (a collection, a table, a partition). Each search is unfiltered within its index, so recall is normal and isolation is physical. The cost is per-index overhead: Qdrant's docs say a collection per tenant is rarely efficient and Qdrant Cloud limits a cluster to 1,000 collections by default; Milvus allows up to 65,536 collections per cluster by default.
2. **Shared index plus a tenant filter**: lessons 1 to 4 apply as they stand. pgvector warns that sharing an approximate index means one tenant's vectors can affect recall and speed for others, and recommends list partitioning or separate tables.
3. **Shared collection, per-tenant graphs**: Qdrant's payload partitioning, below.
4. **One shard per tenant inside one collection**: Weaviate's native multi-tenancy, where each tenant is stored on its own shard.

blocks.title: Four ways to lay out tenants

scenes.caption: Layout 1, index per tenant (Qdrant collections, Milvus collections or partitions, pgvector partitions): route by tenant and search unfiltered. Exact isolation, per-index overhead.
Layout 2, one shared graph plus the tenant filter: everything from lessons 1 to 4. Selectivity is the tenant's share of the collection, tiny for most tenants.
Layout 3, Qdrant payload partitioning: payload_m = 16 and m = 0 build links only inside each tenant, with no global graph. Tenant searches walk their own links; global searches get slower.
Layout 4, shards: Weaviate gives every tenant its own shard. Qdrant's tiered multitenancy keeps small tenants together in a fallback shard and promotes large ones to dedicated shards.

blocks.md:
**Qdrant payload partitioning** keeps all tenants in one collection with a keyword index on the tenant field. Marking it `is_tenant: true` makes Qdrant store each tenant's points together so they are read sequentially. Setting `payload_m` to a non-zero value such as 16 and `m` to 0 disables the global HNSW graph and builds links per tenant only, which the docs say speeds up indexing a lot. The costs: queries without a tenant filter are slower, since they must scan all groups, and keyword-scoring statistics (BM25, and IDF: how rare a term is across documents) are shared across tenants unless scoped per tenant.

**Milvus's partition key** hashes tenants into 16 physical partitions by default. Each partition holds many tenants, so Milvus evaluates the tenant filter on every entity in the searched partition, and its docs recommend a scalar index on the key.

**Weaviate** stores each tenant on a separate shard and requires the tenant name on every query. Tenants can be set inactive (kept on disk) or offloaded to cloud storage, so idle customers cost little memory. Its docs recommend the **flat** index when objects per index are few, as in multi-tenancy, and offer a **dynamic** index that starts flat and switches to HNSW once a tenant passes a threshold (10,000 objects by default).

**Qdrant's tiered multitenancy** mixes layouts: small tenants share a fallback shard and are separated by a payload filter; a tenant that grows is promoted to a dedicated shard. The docs recommend promoting at about 20,000 points, the same as a collection's indexing threshold, and advise against more than about a thousand dedicated shards per cluster.

Now a skewed population. Take 10,000 tenants and 50 million vectors, with sizes following Zipf's law with exponent 1: tenant number i has size proportional to 1/i. A script gives: the largest tenant holds 5,108,501 vectors (s = 0.10), the 10th 510,850, the 100th 51,085, the 1,000th 5,109 and the smallest 511. The median tenant has about 1,021 vectors, s = 0.00002.

scenes.caption: How many tenants fall in each size band: 4,889 under 1,000 vectors, 4,601 more under 10,000, 383 under 40,000, 122 under a million, and 5 giants.
The share of all vectors in each band (percent): 6.9, 23.5, 14.2, 32.1 and 23.3. The 127 tenants at or above 40,000 vectors hold 55.4% of the data; the other 9,873 hold 44.6%.

blocks.md:
Read the layouts against those numbers:

- **Shared HNSW, post-filtered**: the median tenant's s is 0.00002, so 40 candidates hold 0.0008 matches on average. Unusable without a pre-filter path.
- **Shared collection with Weaviate's planner**: 9,873 tenants sit under the 40,000 `flatSearchCutoff`, so their queries become exact flat scans of at most 40,000 vectors. Only the 127 large tenants walk the shared graph, at s from 0.0008 to 0.1, the range where lesson 3's fragmentation and filter strategies matter.
- **A shard per tenant**: every search is unfiltered. With the dynamic index, 9,490 tenants under 10,000 objects stay flat (exact, at most 10,000 distances) and 510 get their own HNSW.
- **Tiered**: promoting at Qdrant's recommended 20,000 points gives one fallback shard for 9,745 small tenants and 255 dedicated shards, well under the advice of about a thousand.

blocks.prompt: In the tiered layout, the fallback shard holds about 18.7 million vectors from 9,745 small tenants. A query from a 1,000-vector tenant arrives. Which of this course's plans answers it, and roughly how much work does it do?
blocks.reveal: Its selectivity inside the shard is 1,000 / 18.7 million, about 0.00005, so a graph walk would be hopeless. But the tenant field is indexed, so the planner sees a tiny match count and takes the **pre-filter** path: fetch the 1,000 ids from the payload index and score them exactly. In Qdrant terms, 1,000 points of 768-d is 3,000 KB, under the 10,000 KB `full_scan_threshold`. About 1,000 distance computations, recall 1.0.

blocks.md: Per-tenant graphs and shards make cross-tenant search expensive. If the product needs global queries (an admin search, analytics across customers), Qdrant documents that global requests without the tenant filter are slower, and Weaviate's multi-tenant collections require a tenant name on every query. Decide that requirement before choosing a layout.

The tenant filter is a selectivity distribution, not one number. Small tenants want exact scans, large ones want their own graph, and the shared graph with a filter only fits the middle. Tiered layouts exist because real tenant sizes are skewed.

blocks.question: A few tenants hold 60% of your vectors and thousands of tenants hold under 1,000 each. Global search is never needed. Which layout fits best?
options: One shared HNSW graph with post-filtering and a large ef_search
A separate collection for every tenant, thousands of them
Tiered: small tenants share a shard and are answered by exact scans of their matches; the few large tenants get dedicated shards with their own graphs
One shared graph with ACORN for every tenant, because it is predicate-agnostic
blocks.explain: Post-filtering fails at tiny selectivities, and thousands of collections run into per-collection overhead and default limits. A shared graph with ACORN works but makes small tenants walk a huge graph for a few hundred matches an exact scan answers. Tiered layouts give each size the plan it needs.

blocks.question: Why does the pgvector README recommend list partitioning by tenant instead of one HNSW index with WHERE tenant_id = X?
options: Partitioned tables cannot be post-filtered
A shared approximate index lets one tenant's vectors affect another's recall and speed; per-tenant partitions give each tenant its own index
pgvector cannot build HNSW indexes on tables with more than one tenant
List partitioning compresses vectors
blocks.explain: In a shared index, a small tenant's rows are a tiny fraction of the candidates the scan produces, so post-filtering returns few rows and iterative scans must read far. A partition per tenant means each search runs on that tenant's own index, unfiltered.
